question: When do we replay a rally? List every situation that counts as a let.

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) what happens when a rally is replayed, and (2) every situation that counts as a let. Law 14.3 answers the replay part directly. Law 14.2 introduces the list of lets, and reading it shows sub-clauses 14.2.1 through 14.2.7; 14.2.3 ends with a colon and its sub-clauses 14.2.3.1 and 14.2.3.2 supply the two net situations. Law 14.1 says who calls the let. ITTO 5.9.1.2 adds a relevant umpire instruction that a shuttle from an adjacent court is not automatically a let. A search for any further let clauses (e.g., a 14.2.8) returned nothing beyond 14.2.7, so the list is complete as given. All sources are Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, except the ITTO 7.0 (5) instruction.
answer.answer: When a let occurs, the rally is replayed: play since the last service does not count and the player who served last serves again (Law 14.3, Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26). A 'let' is called by the umpire, or by a player if there is no umpire, to halt play (Law 14.1). Under Law 14.2 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, it shall be a 'let' if: (1) the server serves before the receiver is ready (Law 9.4) [14.2.1]; (2) during service, the receiver and the server are both faulted [14.2.2]; (3) after the service is returned, the shuttle is caught on the net and remains suspended on its top [14.2.3.1], or, after passing over the net, is caught in the net [14.2.3.2]; (4) during play, the shuttle disintegrates and the base completely separates from the rest of the shuttle [14.2.4]; (5) in the opinion of the umpire, play is disrupted or a player of the opposing side is distracted by a coach [14.2.5]; (6) a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision [14.2.6]; or (7) any unforeseen or accidental situation has occurred [14.2.7]. Additionally, per Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.9.1.2, a shuttle coming onto the court from an adjacent court is not automatically a let: no let is called if, in the umpire's opinion, the shuttle has not obstructed or distracted the players.

question: My partner cut his hand mid-game and it's bleeding. How long can we stop, and who can come on court to help?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) how long play can stop for a bleeding injury, and (2) who may come on court to help. The given sources cover both. For duration: itto-5.14.2 gives the specific rule for a blood-flowing injury (delay until bleeding stops, wound dressed, or Referee advises otherwise); itto-3.6.1.4 requires the Referee to resolve the situation as quickly as possible and well within a few minutes; itto-5.14.1 and itto-3.6.1.2 prohibit treatment causing undue delay on court (quick relief like a bandage is allowed, time-consuming treatment only in regular intervals); itto-5.14.1 and itto-3.6.1.1 say the Umpire times the delay. For who comes on court: itto-3.6.1.1 says the Referee and Tournament Doctor go on court immediately when called; itto-5.14.1 says the Referee decides whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required; itto-3.6.1.3 allows a maximum of two persons on court to assist/advise/translate, with the same consideration for the opposing side. A follow-up search confirmed no additional time limit exists beyond these clauses. All from Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26.
answer.answer: How long you can stop: For a blood-flowing injury, the game is delayed until the bleeding stops, the wound is suitably dressed, or the Referee advises the Umpire otherwise [itto-5.14.2]. The Referee must resolve the injury situation as quickly as possible and well within a few minutes so play can be resumed or abandoned, and may point to potential disqualification if the player is suspected of exploiting the injury to regain wind or repeatedly hesitates in deciding to continue or abandon [itto-3.6.1.4]. No treatment causing undue delay is given on court [itto-5.14.1]; the Tournament Doctor may apply quick relief such as a bandage on a bleeding injury, but no time-consuming treatment is allowed except in the regular intervals, and only if it can be completed (or nearly so) before the interval ends [itto-3.6.1.2]. The Umpire times the delay caused by the injury [itto-5.14.1, itto-3.6.1.1]. Who can come on court: When called by the Umpire, the Referee and the Tournament Doctor immediately go on court [itto-3.6.1.1]; the Referee decides whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required on court [itto-5.14.1]. The Referee may allow a maximum of two persons on court to assist and advise the injured player and help with translation, and in fairness must allow the opposing side the same consideration [itto-3.6.1.3]. All rules are from the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26.

The Referee shall resolve the injury situation as quickly as possible and well within a few minutes so that play can be resumed or abandoned. The Referee may need to point to potential disqualification if it is suspected that the player is exploiting the injury situation to regain wind, or if the player repeatedly hesitates in deciding to continue or abandon play.

The Referee will decide whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required on court (Instruction 3.6). The Tournament Doctor shall examine the player and advise the player about the severity of injury or sickness. No treatment causing undue delay shall be given on court. The Umpire shall time the delay caused by the injury.

When called by the Umpire in case of injury or illness, the Referee and the Tournament Doctor shall immediately go on court. The Referee shall first speak to the Umpire to be informed of the relevant facts and to remind the Umpire to time the delay due to the injury.

The Referee may allow a maximum of two persons on court to assist and advise the injured player and help with translation. In fairness, the Referee shall allow the opposing side the same consideration.

question: Water started dripping from the roof onto our court mid-game. What happens to the match and the score?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens to the match and the score when water makes the court unplayable mid-game. The given sources cover this directly: itto-5.11.3 (court temporarily not playable → call the Referee and suspend until suitable), itto-5.11.2 (suspension warranted by circumstances affecting playing conditions), itto-5.11.4 (announcement and 'S' notation), and itto-5.11.5 (resumption procedure). A search for the score question found laws-16.3.3, which states the existing score stands after suspension. Together these answer both parts of the question, so no refusal is needed.
answer.answer: Water dripping onto the court makes it 'temporarily not playable', so the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play is suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.11.3). More generally, play may be suspended by the Referee or Umpire when warranted by a circumstance affecting playing conditions (ITTO Clause 5.11.2). When play is suspended, the Umpire calls "Play is suspended" and notes "S" on the scoring device or score-sheet (ITTO Clause 5.11.4). The score is not affected: under Law 16.3.3 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, "If play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point." When play resumes, the Umpire notes the duration of the suspension, ensures the players are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then calls "Are you ready?" followed by the score and "Play" (ITTO Clause 5.11.5).

citations.quote: If, during a match, a court or its immediate surroundings needs repair, or it is temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play.
Play may be suspended by the Referee or Umpire if warranted by a circumstance affecting playing conditions.
When play is suspended, the Umpire shall call: “Play is suspended” and note “S” on the scoring device or score-sheet, if used.
If play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point.

When play resumes after the suspension, the Umpire shall note the duration of the suspension and ensure that the players are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then call “Are you ready?” followed by the score and “Play”.

question: My opponent keeps flicking sweat onto the court. What can the umpire do about it?

answer.reasoning: The question is directly covered: ITTO Clause 5.9.1.6 addresses a player throwing sweat/contaminating the court and says the umpire shall remind the player and apply Law 16.7 if necessary. Law 16.7.1 (read because it ends with a colon) lists the umpire's options—warning, fault if previously warned, fault for flagrant offence—and Law 16.7.2 adds that on a fault the umpire must report immediately to the Referee, who may disqualify. No part of the question is unanswered.
answer.answer: Under Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.9.1.6, a player throwing sweat or otherwise contaminating the court and its immediate surroundings shall be reminded that such conduct is unacceptable, with Law 16.7 applied if necessary. Under Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 16.7.1, the umpire administers a breach of Law 16.6 (among others) by issuing a warning to the offending side, or faulting the offending side if previously warned, or faulting the offending side in cases of flagrant offence or breach. Under Law 16.7.2, once the umpire faults a side under Law 16.7.1.2 or 16.7.1.3, the umpire shall report the offending side immediately to the Referee, who has the power to disqualify the offending side from the match.

question: The line judge couldn't see whether the shuttle landed in. What happens to the rally?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens to a rally when the line judge is unsighted. The sources answer this directly: itto-8.5 tells the unsighted Line Judge to signal the Umpire; itto-5.8.3 (with 5.8.3.1–5.8.3.3) states that where a Line Judge is unsighted the Umpire shall immediately call, and gives the exact calls depending on where the shuttle landed and whether the Umpire/IRS can decide; itto-2.5 confirms the Umpire makes the decision when another official is unsighted and that a 'let' is called when no decision can be made unless IRS is in use; laws-14.2.6 states the let condition in the Laws; itto-5.8.9/5.8.9.1 cover the IRS 'NO DECISION' case. Together these fully answer what happens to the rally, so no part is missing and no refusal is needed.
answer.answer: If the Line Judge is unsighted, the Line Judge must first inform the Umpire immediately by putting both hands up to cover the eyes (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 8.5: "If unsighted, inform the Umpire immediately by putting both hands up to cover the eyes."). The Umpire then takes over the line call: "Where there is no Line Judge or if a Line Judge is unsighted, the Umpire shall immediately call:" (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 5.8.3). If the Umpire can see where the shuttle landed, the rally is decided normally — the Umpire calls "Out" when the shuttle lands outside the line and then calls either the score or "Service over" and then the score (Clause 5.8.3.1: ""Out" when the shuttle lands outside the line and then call either the score or "Service over" and then the score;"), or calls the score or "Service over" and then the score when the shuttle lands "in" (Clause 5.8.3.2: "The score or "Service over" and then the score when the shuttle lands "in";"). ITTO Clause 2.5 states the same: "When another official is unsighted, the Umpire shall make the decision. When no decision can be made, a 'let' shall be called (Law 17.6.6), unless IRS is in use, in which case it will be used to decide on the line call". Where an Instant Review System is in operation, the Umpire instead calls "Unsighted" and requests a decision from the system by raising the left hand above the head (Clause 5.8.3.3: "except when an IRS is in operation, the Umpire shall call "Unsighted" and request a decision from the system by raising the left hand above the head."); if the IRS indicates "NO DECISION", it is a "Let" when the original call was "Unsighted" (Clause 5.8.9.1: ""Let" but only for an original call of unsighted;"). So the rally either ends with the Umpire's in/out call and score, or is replayed as a let when neither the Umpire nor the IRS can make a decision.

question: Can my coach get up from his chair and stand at the side of the court during the match?

answer.reasoning: The question is directly answered by ITTO 5.12.2, which states coaches must remain seated and must not stand court-side during the match except during permitted intervals under Law 16.2. Laws 16.2.1 and 16.2.2 define those permitted intervals, so they are relevant to the exception. No search is needed because the provided sources cover the rule and the exception.
answer.answer: No. Under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, a coach must stay in the designated seat and "must not stand court-side during the match except during the permitted intervals (Law 16.2)" [itto-5.12.2]. The permitted intervals under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, are "not exceeding 60 seconds during each game when the leading score reaches 11 points, except Handicap matches" [laws-16.2.1] and "not exceeding 120 seconds between the first and second game, and between the second and third game" [laws-16.2.2]. So the coach may stand court-side only during those intervals, not during play.

answer.answer: A plastic (non-feathered) shuttle must have the same weight as a feathered shuttle — from 4.74 to 5.50 grams — but because of the difference in specific gravity and other properties of synthetic materials, a variation of up to 10 per cent is acceptable (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Clauses 2.3.3 and 2.2.6). question: My opponent got a yellow card for swearing during the warm-up, before the umpire called 'Play'. Does it cost him a point now, and does the card go on his record after the tournament?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) whether a yellow card issued during warm-up before "Play" costs a point in the match, and (2) whether the card is recorded after the tournament. itto-5.17.10 directly covers pre-match misconduct on the Field of Play before "Play": cards given have no effect on the score but are taken into account if further offences occur during the match, cross-referencing Law 16.7.1.2 (faulting the offending side if previously warned). For the record question, itto-3.7.3 covers the Referee's post-tournament report of yellow and red cards to BWF (or CC), with itto-3.7.3.1 noting the Referee may decide not to report a card, and itto-5.17.2 requiring the Umpire to record and report the incident to the Referee. Together these answer both parts; no further search needed.
answer.answer: No, the yellow card does not cost him a point now. Under Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), Clause 5.17.10 (in force 2025-04-26), misconduct before the match while on the Field of Play before "Play" is treated as a warning/red card/black card situation, and "Any card(s) given shall have no effect on the score of the match but a card(s) shall be taken into account if further offences occur during the match (Law 16.7.1.2)". So the pre-match yellow card does not affect the score, but it stays on the books: if he commits a further offence during the match, Law 16.7.1.2 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26) says the umpire administers the breach by "faulting the offending side, if previously warned" — a fault, which costs a point. As for the record after the tournament: yes, the card is reported. The Umpire must "Record and report to the Referee any incident of misconduct and the action taken" (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 5.17.2), and "The Referee shall immediately after the tournament send to BWF (or CC) a report on withdrawals, yellow and red cards, that may trigger further sanctions" (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 3.7.3, under 3.7 After the Tournament). However, the Referee may decide not to report a card "if the Referee or a Deputy has observed the situation where the card was given and decides that the card should not have been issued" (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 3.7.3.1).
